rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four genuinely pitchable lanes, not three, and the extra one is real: "The hard part of a circular sneaker is the mail: On scales a nationwide take-back loop" turns the take-back system into an operations story. B's strongest line, "On's recycled-shoe pledge meets the question it won't answer: how much actually gets remade?", is sharp and probably the punchiest single contrarian angle. But B leaves the reverse-logistics story inside proof bullets instead of making it a beat-ready pitch, while A separates business model, P&L, materials scale-up, and mail-back operations cleanly.
gaps_in_A: The first angle says "a major athletic brand is moving a core product from purchase to subscription nationwide"; "core product" is a stretch from the provided facts, which say Cyclon is launching nationwide, not that it is core to On's lineup.
The materials angle says "pilot volume to nationwide distribution"; that is a fair inference, but it still needs caution because no volumes are disclosed.
A misses B's sharper standalone greenwashing/scrutiny angle around "how much actually gets remade?" It asks the question, but does not shape it as a pitchable contrarian story.
gaps_in_B: B omits a standalone reverse-logistics angle even though the facts hand it one: mail-back, grinding, remaking, national scale. That's a real trade/supply-chain story, not just supporting proof.
B omits the castor-bean materials scale-up story; "third-party verification of the castor-bean material's recyclability" appears only as proof, not as a separate beat.
The next step says "meanest-editor" and "draft a tight pitch" before resolving the missing monthly fee and recycling rate. For angle work, `journalist-fit-check` would be the cleaner next move.

The first angle asks for "one named subscriber or pilot participant" as proof. Useful, but it risks drifting into a customer anecdote the source facts do not provide and that the set correctly refuses elsewhere.
